# Conjugates — Eliminate an Awkward Radical Difference

## The identity to remember

$$
(\sqrt a-\sqrt b)(\sqrt a+\sqrt b)=a-b
$$

**Every symbol explained:** a,b are nonnegative real values; √a is the nonnegative square root; the plus/minus expressions are conjugates. Their product removes both radicals.

**Substitute actual numbers:** Calculate √50−√49 without directly subtracting decimal approximations. Since (√50−7)(√50+7)=1, the difference equals 1/(√50+7)≈0.0711.

## Why it is true

This is the difference-of-squares identity applied with √a and √b as the two bases. Multiplying by the conjugate cancels radicals in the numerator or denominator.

## When to recognise it

Use it for numerical stability when two large, nearly equal square roots are subtracted, and for simplifying limiting expressions. It is a genuine computational technique, not just an algebra exam trick.

## Algorithm or number puzzle application

For a=10001,b=10000, √10001−100 = 1/(√10001+100), approximately 0.005; direct subtraction of rounded roots can lose precision.

## Assumptions and pitfalls

If a and b are real and negative, their principal square roots are not real; the formula needs appropriate complex-number conventions. Never divide by a zero conjugate.

## Your turn

Rationalise √65−8 and compare it with 1/16.

**Memory rule:** Understand the cancellation or construction that produces the identity. Re-derive the rule from two small numbers, then say aloud when you would use it.
